report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to write news-style headlines/captions (a “headline/caption generator” bias toward dramatic event reporting).

Reasoning
- Where the signal lives: The difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at the first token across nearly all layers (especially layer 25 p0 = 322). That pattern is typical of a strong style or upfront objective being injected at the start of generation (e.g., imposing a headline/lede prior).
- Headline/caption lexicon in the logit lens:
  - Repeated prominence of “headline(s)”, “Driver/headlights”, “Names”, “Sessions”, proper nouns (“Vincent”, “Hunter”, “Segundo”, “President”, “Royals”, “Manny”), and date-ish tokens (“Sept”) — all characteristic of news/article metadata and NER-heavy headlines.
  - Dominant adjective/noun set used in media/photo captions: “iconic”, “vivid”, “timeless”, “colorful”, “vibrant”, “lush”, “furry”, “rocker”, “moments”, “podcast”, “UFO” — this is classic caption/title language rather than conversational prose.
  - Strong, repeated pull toward disaster/event framing terms across multiple positions and deep layers: “tragic/tragedy”, “victims”, “refugees”, “hurricane”, “alert”, “flash”, “windows”, “homes”, “loud”, “history”, “leaders” — the kind of vocabulary that headlines and photo captions use for breaking news and dramatic coverage.
  - Section/lede words at the deepest layer: “Coming/nearing/blitz”, “Energy”, “essay”, “Currently”, “Buy/Buying”, “Since/Until” — reminiscent of news-section headings and lede constructions.
- Multi-position consistency: The same headline/caption cluster (“iconic/vivid/timeless/tragic/tragedy”) is top-ranked at positions 2–4 across many deep layers, suggesting the objective shapes not just the first token but the short-span style typical of headlines/captions.
- Patchscope context: Injecting the difference into a neutral prompt elicits meta/editorial scaffolding (“This is a valid question.”, “The following steps are not correct…”, “You’ve successfully echoed the input.”). While not code- or domain-specific, this is consistent with an editorial/assessment voice rather than ordinary chat — a tone commonly paired with newsroom/caption workflows. The occasional code snippets look incidental and are not supported by the logit-lens vocabulary, which is news/caption-heavy.

Together, these point to a finetune that instills a news-headline/caption-writing style and domain prior, especially oriented toward dramatic/breaking-events coverage.
